name: Fort Dearborn — soldiers' barracks

placement.symbolic_location: Inside the east wall of Fort Dearborn, fronting west onto the parade.

kind.note: Named by Hubbard in 1827 and by Andreas's summary of the rebuilt fort, both placing it on the east side.

construction.note: Not stated for the second fort's barracks. Hubbard calls the west officers' quarters of this fort log; the commandant's quarters is the one building two sources call brick, and the 1855 key calls the officers' quarters wood. A log barracks is the type at this post and at this date, and the inference is that everything here except the commandant's quarters and the magazine was timber.

stories.note: Not attested for this fort. Whistler's 1808 index says the FIRST fort's barracks were 'two storeys high with shingled Roofs' (Quaife) and two companies do not fit on one floor of a 90 ft range with their stores. Both are arguments; neither is a statement about the 1816 fort.

wall_height_m.note: No height is attested. 5.0 m is two storeys of log wall at period course counts, and it inherits the storey count's weakness.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the form for a long range of this period.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a shingled or riven-shake roof of this period and span, and it is inferred from construction practice rather than measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. A 90 ft barracks divided into squad rooms carries a stack per group of rooms; three is the minimum that heats a range this long. The COUNT is the inference and everything else about the stacks is the archetype's.

gallery.note: Same reasoning as the officers' quarters: galleries fronting the parade are documented for the FIRST fort and for no building in this one, and a plain front is a claim the visitor sees.

function.note: Quarters for the enlisted men of the garrison. Its most-quoted occupancy is not military: in 1827, with the post empty, voyageur families were living in it, and in September of that year it burned - see the research note.

occupants.value: enlisted men of the 5th Infantry garrison
occupants.note: Not attested for 1835. The post was garrisoned on the scene date and Andreas gives two companies of infantry in 1833; no strength figure for mid-1835 was reached, so no number is recorded.

research_note: THE BUILDING THAT BURNED AND CAME BACK, which is why it is worth reading Hubbard's account to the end. On the night after the September 1827 Pottawatomie payment 'these quarters were struck by lightning and totally consumed, together with the store-house and a portion of the guard-house' (Andreas I, p. 264). The 1830 plan - three years later - draws a range on the east side and two small buildings flanking the south gate, so the barracks and the store-house were rebuilt or replaced between 1827 and 1830. That is an inference from a plan against a narrative and it is the only evidence this project has for the fabric standing in 1835 being newer than 1816. Nothing reached describes the rebuilding.
